---
title: "The same container for any type"
---

Every class you have written so far knows exactly what it holds. Write one that
keeps a pile of numbers and you have solved the problem for numbers, and for
nothing else. The day you need the same pile for strings you have two options:
copy the file, or leave the type open. TypeScript has the second one, and you
have been using it since Part 2 without a name for it.

Generics are new for the coding buddy as well. Part 6 has one that writes
them, and its key replaces the Part 5 key in `~/.pi/agent/auth.json`
(@sec-buddy-setup-new-part).

{{< coding coding-buddy-generics >}}

## Two stacks, one difference {#sec-generics-experiment}

A **stack** is a pile. You put a value on top, and the value you take off is
the one you put on last. Undo buttons work that way, and so does the back
button of your browser.

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `generics`. Delete `src/math.test.ts`.

2. Write `src/number-stack.ts`:

   ```ts
   export class NumberStack {
     private items: number[] = [];

     push(item: number): void {
       this.items.push(item);
     }

     pop(): number | undefined {
       return this.items.pop();
     }

     peek(): number | undefined {
       return this.items[this.items.length - 1];
     }

     get size(): number {
       return this.items.length;
     }
   }
   ```

3. Next to it, write `src/number-stack.test.ts`:

   ```ts
   import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
   import { NumberStack } from './number-stack';

   describe('NumberStack', () => {
     it('starts empty', () => {
       const stack = new NumberStack();

       expect(stack.size).toBe(0);
     });

     it('gives the last pushed value back first', () => {
       const stack = new NumberStack();
       stack.push(1);
       stack.push(2);

       expect(stack.pop()).toBe(2);
       expect(stack.pop()).toBe(1);
     });

     it('pops undefined when it is empty', () => {
       const stack = new NumberStack();

       expect(stack.pop()).toBeUndefined();
     });
   });
   ```

4. Run `npm test`:

   ```text
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)
   ```

5. Now the app needs the same pile for strings. Copy `src/number-stack.ts` to
   `src/string-stack.ts`, rename the class to `StringStack`, and replace every
   `number` that describes the content with `string`.

Count the edits in the copy. There are four: the field, the parameter of
`push`, and the return types of `pop` and `peek`. The getter stays `number`,
because it counts items instead of holding them. Every other line, all the
logic, is character for character the same. And the test file needs the same
treatment, another copy with another handful of renames.

Two files that differ in four words are two files that drift apart. Fix a bug
in one, forget the other. Throw both away and write one file that leaves the
content type open.

6. Write `src/stack.ts`:

   ```ts
   export class Stack<T> {
     private items: T[] = [];

     push(item: T): void {
       this.items.push(item);
     }

     pop(): T | undefined {
       return this.items.pop();
     }

     peek(): T | undefined {
       return this.items[this.items.length - 1];
     }

     get size(): number {
       return this.items.length;
     }
   }
   ```

7. Delete `src/number-stack.ts` and `src/string-stack.ts`. Rename the test file
   to `src/stack.test.ts`, change its import line to

   ```ts
   import { Stack } from './stack';
   ```

   and replace every `new NumberStack()` with `new Stack<number>()`. Shorten
   the `describe` title to `'Stack'` while you are there. Everything else, the
   calls and the expected values, stays as it is.

8. Run `npm test`:

   ```text
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)
   ```

## One class with a hole in it {#sec-generics-type-parameter}

`<T>` after the class name of `Stack` declares a **type parameter**. It is a
name for a type that the class does not pick, so the class is a blueprint with
one hole in it, and the caller fills the hole. `new Stack<number>()` fills `T` with
`number` for that one object, `new Stack<string>()` fills it with `string`, and
`new Stack<Shape>()` would give you a pile of shapes. The `T` is just a name,
the way `item` is a name for a parameter.

The checking is real. Open `src/index.ts`, replace everything in it with these
lines, and run `npx tsc --noEmit`:

```ts
import { Stack } from './stack';

const numbers = new Stack<number>();
numbers.push(7);
numbers.push('seven');
```

```text
src/index.ts(5,14): error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.
```

Inside the class, `push` takes a `T`. At this call site `T` is `number`, so
`'seven'` is refused, exactly as it was in `NumberStack`. Delete the last line.

Leave the angle brackets off completely and `new Stack()` still compiles, but
`T` becomes `unknown`, the type you met in a `catch`, and every check you
wanted is gone. This class has no constructor argument, so TypeScript has
nothing to read the type from. Put it in the angle brackets every time.

One detail about the two `| undefined`. `pop` gets it from `Array.pop()`, which
has nothing to hand back when the array is empty. `peek` gets it from
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in `tsconfig.json`, the setting that treats every
array index as possibly past the end. Neither of them is ever `null`.

## Functions get type parameters too {#sec-generics-functions}

A function can leave a type open too, the same way `Stack` does. In an arrow
function the `<T>` goes in front of the parameter list. Add this to
`src/index.ts`, run `npm start`, and open the browser console with F12:

```ts
const first = <T>(items: T[]): T | undefined => {
  return items[0];
};

console.log(first([3, 1, 2]));
console.log(first<string>([]));
```

The console shows `3` and then `undefined`.

The first call has no angle brackets at all. TypeScript read the argument, saw
a `number[]`, and filled `T` with `number` by itself; hover over the call in VS
Code and it tells you the result is `number | undefined`. That is **inference**,
and it is why `push` has been guarding your arrays since year one without you
ever naming a type.

The second call hands over an empty array, and an empty array says nothing
about what belongs in it. There is nothing to read, so you say it yourself.

## A type parameter with a promise attached {#sec-generics-constraints}

Say you want one line of text per item, from anything that can describe itself.
Add a small class and a second function to `src/index.ts`:

```ts
class Rect {
  constructor(
    private width: number,
    private height: number,
  ) {}

  describe(): string {
    return `Rectangle ${this.width} by ${this.height}`;
  }
}

const describeAll = <T>(items: T[]): string[] => {
  const lines: string[] = [];
  for (const item of items) {
    lines.push(item.describe());
  }
  return lines;
};
```

Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and it refuses, printing the file and the line in front
of this message:

```text
error TS2339: Property 'describe' does not exist on type 'T'.
```

Two more complaints come with it, saying that `Rect` and `describeAll` are
never used. Both are true right now and both disappear as soon as the call
below exists, so read past them here.

TypeScript is right. `T` is whatever the caller picks, and a `T` that turns out
to be `number` has no `describe`. So say what the function needs from `T`,
without asking for a whole class:

```ts
const describeAll = <T extends { describe(): string }>(items: T[]): string[] => {
```

`extends` in angle brackets is a **constraint** rather than a base class. It
means "at least this shape": any type with a `describe()` method that returns a
string may fill `T`, and TypeScript checks that at every call. Inside the
function you may now call `describe()` and nothing else, because that is the
whole promise.

Call it and watch the console:

```ts
for (const line of describeAll([new Rect(30, 20), new Rect(10, 10)])) {
  console.log(line);
}
```

```text
Rectangle 30 by 20
Rectangle 10 by 10
```

The `Shape` classes from Part 4 fit this constraint without a single change,
because the abstract `Shape` promises `describe()` to everyone who extends it.

## The generics you already use {#sec-generics-known}

Angle brackets have been in your code since Part 2, and every one of them was a
type parameter getting filled in.

`number[]` is the short spelling of `Array<number>`. The array class leaves its
content type open, and you fill it in every time you write a type annotation.

`new Map<string, number>()` from Part 4 fills two holes, one for the keys and
one for the values, and `new Set<string>()` fills one. A class may have as many
type parameters as it needs, separated by commas, which is what the exercise
below builds.

`document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('#addShape')` is a generic function.
Nothing in the text `'#addShape'` tells TypeScript what kind of element comes
back, so you fill the hole yourself, exactly as `first<string>([])` does.

One more is waiting for you. `Promise<T>` is what code hands back while it is
still busy fetching something, and you meet it when this course starts loading
data from the network.

::: {.research title="Three things this chapter leaves to you"}
The exercise below picks a random item out of an array, and one of its tests
checks that the picked item really came from that array. Two of the answers
live on MDN, on the pages for
[`Math.random()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math/random)
and [`Math.floor()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math/floor);
the third is on the
[`expect` page of the Vitest documentation](https://vitest.dev/api/expect).

1. Which is the smallest number `Math.random()` can return, which is the
   largest, and which of those two ends can actually come out? Then say why
   `Math.random() * items.length` never reaches `items.length`.
2. `Math.floor` and `Math.round` both turn a number with decimals into a whole
   number. What does each of them give for `2.7` and for `2.2`, and which of
   the two never answers with a larger whole number than it was handed?
3. Which Vitest matcher checks that an array contains a given value, and what
   does the same matcher check when you hand it a string instead of an array?

Questions 1 and 2 are exam material. Picking a random item out of an array
shows up in almost every task, and the exam has no internet and no AI.
:::

## Exercise: random shapes {#sec-generics-exercise}

The shape generator from @sec-svg-dom-exercise gets a **Surprise me** button.
One click picks a shape kind and a color that belong together, then drops that
shape somewhere on the canvas.

{{< exercise shape-generator tests=true >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `random-shapes`.

2. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`. The `index.html` you copied in
   has no place for `add` any more.

3. In `index.html`, add a third button right after **Clear all**:

   ```html
   <button id="surpriseButton" type="button">Surprise me</button>
   ```

4. Create `src/shape-kind.ts` with one line:

   ```ts
   export type ShapeKind = 'circle' | 'rect';
   ```

5. Write the test file `src/pair.test.ts` before the class it tests. As with
   the bracelet rules in the Vitest chapter, the list below describes the
   tests and the code is yours to write. One `describe('Pair', ...)` with
   three `it`s, each of them building its pair
   with `new Pair<string, number>('circle', 3)`:

   * the pair keeps `'circle'` in `first` and `3` in `second`;
   * `swap()` gives back a pair whose `first` is `3` and whose `second` is
     `'circle'`;
   * the original pair still has `'circle'` in `first` after a `swap()`.

6. Write `src/pair.ts`. A class may declare more than one type parameter, and
   `Pair` needs two:

   ```ts
   export class Pair<A, B> {
     constructor(
       readonly first: A,
       readonly second: B,
     ) {}

     // swap() goes here
   }
   ```

   Add a `swap()` method whose return type is `Pair<B, A>`, a new pair holding
   the same two values the other way round. Run `npm test`. Expected result:

   ```text
    Tests  3 passed (3)
   ```

7. Write `src/random.ts` with two exported helpers. `randomBetween(min, max)`
   is the one you wrote in the shape generator chapter, unchanged. The second
   one is new:

   ```ts
   export const pickRandom = <T>(items: T[]): T | undefined => {
     // one line: read items at a random whole index
   };
   ```

   The research box has both pieces you need to build that index, and the
   reason it never points past the end of the array.

8. Write `src/random.test.ts` with four `it`s for `pickRandom`: an empty array
   gives `undefined`; `['circle']` gives `'circle'`; a pick out of
   `['red', 'green', 'blue']` is one of those three, checked with the matcher
   from the research box; and the type survives the pick, which these two lines
   show:

   ```ts
   const kinds: ShapeKind[] = ['circle', 'rect'];
   const kind: ShapeKind | undefined = pickRandom(kinds);
   ```

   The second line only compiles because `pickRandom` hands back the same type
   it was given. Check with the same matcher that `kind` is one of the two
   kinds. Run `npm test`. Expected result:

   ```text
    Test Files  2 passed (2)
         Tests  7 passed (7)
   ```

9. Write `src/index.ts`. Copy it from your own shape generator project in
   `coursework/`, or build it again from steps 2 to 9 of
   @sec-svg-dom-exercise. Then delete its local `randomBetween` and import that
   helper from `./random` instead. Run `npm start`. Expected result: the
   toolbar works as it did before, and **Surprise me** does nothing yet.

10. The helper that adds one shape still decides the kind and the color by
    reading `shapeKind.value` and `shapeColor.value` inside. Give it two more
    parameters, `kind: string` and `color: string`, and use them in place of
    the two `.value` reads. The **Add shape** listener now passes
    `shapeKind.value` and `shapeColor.value` in. Run `npm start`. Expected
    result: the toolbar behaves exactly as before.

11. Look up the new button with the others, take it into the same `if` that
    throws, and put the presets under the element lookups:

    ```ts
    const presets: Pair<ShapeKind, string>[] = [
      new Pair('circle', '#e63946'),
      new Pair('rect', '#457b9d'),
      new Pair('circle', '#f4a261'),
      new Pair('rect', '#2a9d8f'),
    ];
    ```

    Listen for a click on the **Surprise me** button. Pick one preset with
    `pickRandom`, leave the handler at once when the result is `undefined`, and
    otherwise call your helper with `preset.first`, `preset.second`, and a
    random position. Expected result: every click drops one shape, and its
    kind and its color always come from the same preset.

12. Add the `verify` script to `package.json` as in every new app, run
    `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.
